A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same provider-bias study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments across seven LLMs, comparisons of debiasing prompts, a 39-developer questionnaire, and a 50-participant human study.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and additionally reports manual validation of 10,000 labeled responses and scenario-specific modification rates.

M1.justification: The prompt-generation pipeline, GPT-4o initial-code generation, response filtering, feature-based labeling with GPT-4o fallback, and seven mitigation prompts remain unchanged. The added manual audit evaluates labeling accuracy without establishing a change to the labeling algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions retain six coding tasks, 30 scenarios, 145 requirements, Python generation and Python-to-Java translation, and the same questionnaire and human-study coverage. The new labeling audit and scenario analysis use the existing corpus.

E2.justification: The same seven LLMs are evaluated. Table 2 retains Original, COT, Debias, Quick Answer, Simple, Multiple, Ask-General, and Ask-Specific, with no comparator added or removed.

E3.justification: v2 newly reports a validation protocol involving two expert co-authors manually checking 10,000 randomly selected labeled cases (A.2.4). The main experiments retain their model versions, metrics, prompt subsets, and query budgets. Additional participant qualifications document the retained studies without establishing that their cohorts changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds a labeling-accuracy audit and an analysis of modification frequency across scenarios, highlighting Data Visualization and Container Orchestration. Existing human-study analyses, modification case studies, model-capability correlations, and comparisons with conversational preferences remain, often relocated.

E5.justification: Statistical reporting changes slightly: v2 explicitly identifies a t-test for target-provider frequency comparisons in A.3.3, while v1's explicit paired t-test report for between-model GI comparisons is omitted. The 20/5-query repetition counts and 1,000-sample bootstrap strategy remain unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds no reported labeling errors in 10,000 audited cases and modification rates of 12.10% for Data Visualization and 0.10% for Container Orchestration. It removes v1's detailed correlation matrix and some explicit results, including translation/debugging modification rates of 5.20%/3.00%. Every numerical row in Table 2 is unchanged.

T1.justification: The provider-bias definition and GI/MR formulas are retained, with some explanations moved or repeated in the appendices. Percentage wording changes do not alter the metric definitions. Neither version introduces theoretical proofs or theorems.

C1.justification: Both versions claim the first empirical investigation of provider bias in LLM code generation, an automated dataset pipeline, preferences favoring Google and Amazon, unsolicited service substitutions, and difficulty mitigating bias through prompting. Rewriting and reduced prominence of the internal-knowledge comparison do not remove its retained findings.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explicit limitation that quantifying and comparing bias across LLMs is not the study's intended goal. It also interprets the new scenario-level findings, suggesting that substitutions in Data Visualization can reflect switching paid services to simpler Python-library implementations. Existing market-share and programming-language caveats remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses online, unpaid study administration, participant education/experience requirements, absence of demographic collection, and approximately 70 hours per reviewer for the labeling audit. It replaces the anonymous repository link with a named GitHub repository link. Model identifiers, hardware, and existing prompt templates remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on code/social bias and personalization, including Mouselinos et al., Gupta et al., and Vijjini et al., while pruning earlier recommender-system references such as FairEvalLLM. It also changes the market-share source to Hava (2024). The central distinction between provider bias and prior social-bias research remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative are extensively condensed and rewritten. Related Work moves from Section 6 to Section 2; the motivation and internal-knowledge comparison move into appendices. The RQ/finding-based organization is recast, and separate Limitation and Ethical Considerations sections are added. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: The manuscript undergoes extensive typesetting, table-sizing, caption, and figure-placement changes. Numerous figures move into appendices, and Table 2 adds metric-direction arrows. v1's correlation heatmap disappears; its standalone conversational-preference chart is also omitted, although those chart results remain in v2's combined comparison figure.

improvement.justification: v1 describes automated labeling without an accuracy audit; v2 reports two authors checking 10,000 cases without finding mislabeling. This adds useful validation, while participant disclosures and explicit scope limitations improve transparency. These gains are partly offset by losing the detailed correlation evidence in v1 Fig. 14; the core experiments and findings remain largely unchanged.
